power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Comparing Webcam-Based and Infrared Eye Tracking in Educational Research: Data Quality, Measurement Agreement, and Usability Across Dynamic and Static Stimuli
table.research_questions:
RQ1: Do accuracy and precision of eye tracking data differ between a webcam-based eye tracking system (Labvanced) and an infrared (IR) eye tracking system (Tobii Pro Spectrum), and do key eye tracking metrics derived from both systems differ systematically?

H1a: The IR system yields higher spatial accuracy than the webcam-based system, i.e., a smaller mean angular offset (in degrees of visual angle) between recorded gaze positions and target positions.

H1b: The IR system yields higher spatial precision than the webcam-based system, i.e., a smaller sample-to-sample root mean square deviation (RMS, in degrees of visual angle).

H1c: Despite the lower data quality of the webcam-based system, key eye tracking metrics derived from the classroom video vignettes (number of fixations, mean fixation duration, mean saccade length, and number of AOI hits on predefined student and teacher AOIs) differ only marginally between the two systems. Specifically, we expect the differences between systems to lie within equivalence bounds of d = ±0.30.

RQ2: Does the recording environment (laboratory vs. home) affect the data quality of webcam-based eye tracking?

H2a: Webcam-based recordings conducted at home show lower accuracy and lower precision than webcam-based recordings conducted in the laboratory.

H2b: Webcam-based recordings conducted at home show greater between-participant variability in eye tracking metrics (number of fixations, mean fixation duration, mean saccade length, number of AOI hits) than webcam-based recordings conducted in the laboratory.

H2c: The difference in data quality between the webcam-based and the IR system is larger for participants who completed the webcam recording at home than for participants who completed both recordings in the laboratory (interaction of eye tracking system × recording environment).

The graph interpretation task is not part of the confirmatory hypotheses and will be analyzed exploratively.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Authors have observed the data, but have not performed the proposed analyses. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan has been accessed and observed by the authors. The authors have sufficiently observed relevant evidence to influence their analysis decisions or conclusions. However, the authors have not yet performed any of the proposed analyses in this plan and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
table.additional_blinding_during_research_or_a: Blinding of participants and experimenters is not possible in this study, since the eye tracking system and the recording environment are inherently visible to everyone involved. To minimize unintended influences, we rely on standardized and automated procedures instead. During data collection, all participants received standardized written instructions, and each recording started with a system-specific calibration that was repeated when calibration quality was insufficient. Participants were not informed about the hypotheses of the study. The stimuli did not require any responses, so participant behavior during the task was not subject to experimenter evaluation. For data analysis, no subjective coding is involved: fixations, saccades, and AOI hits will be derived algorithmically from the raw gaze data using identical event detection parameters for both systems, which are specified in this preregistration prior to analysis. The areas of interest were defined in advance based on prior studies with the same video vignettes and are identical for both systems. Data exclusion criteria are likewise specified in advance and will be applied uniformly to both systems and both recording environments.
table.stimuli_description: The main stimuli consist of five short video vignettes (approximately one minute each) showing authentic whole-class teaching situations from a secondary school mathematics lesson, in which a teacher teaches a class of 24 students about matrix computation. The vignettes were recorded in a previous DFG-funded project and have been used in several earlier eye tracking studies on teachers' visual expertise, in which participants rated them as authentic and realistic. For these vignettes, areas of interest (AOIs) for individual students, the teacher, and the learning materials had already been defined in prior work. The same AOI definitions are used for both eye tracking systems. All vignettes were presented full screen, in identical form, and in the same sequence in both recording sessions. Participants were instructed to watch each video carefully as if they were observing a real classroom; no responses were required during viewing. In addition, participants completed a static graph interpretation task, which is analyzed exploratively and is not part of the confirmatory hypotheses. For the assessment of accuracy and precision, gaze data recorded while participants fixated known target positions during the system-specific calibration and validation procedures are used.
table.inter_trial_interval: The video vignettes were presented sequentially. Short breaks were included between vignettes to prevent fatigue and to maintain participant attentiveness. Each recording session started with a system-specific calibration, which was repeated whenever calibration quality was insufficient.
table.eye_tracker_type: Two eye tracking systems were used. (1) Stationary, screen-based infrared eye tracker: Tobii Pro Spectrum (Tobii AB, Danderyd, Sweden), recording binocularly at a sampling frequency of 1200 Hz, operated in the laboratory of the Chair of Educational Psychology at the Technical University of Munich. (2) Web-based eye tracking: Labvanced webcam-based eye tracking (Scicovery GmbH, Osnabrück, Germany), running in the Google Chrome browser. In the home condition, the participants' own laptop or desktop webcams were used; in the laboratory condition, the webcam session took place on a laboratory computer. Gaze is estimated in real time from the webcam video stream; no video recordings of participants are stored. The effective sampling frequency of the webcam-based system depends on the webcam and computer hardware and is therefore variable across participants (typically around 30 Hz); the actual sampling frequency per recording will be reported.
table.display_screen_size: Infrared condition: Stimuli were presented on the 23.8-inch display integrated with the Tobii Pro Spectrum (resolution 1920 × 1080 pixels). Webcam condition in the laboratory: Stimuli were presented on a laboratory computer screen. Webcam condition at home: Stimuli were presented on the participants' own laptop or desktop screens; screen size and resolution therefore varied across participants. Participants were required to use a laptop or desktop computer; tablets and smartphones were not permitted. Screen resolution as reported by the browser is recorded for each webcam session.
table.head_movement_restrictions: No chin rest or other physical head restraint was used in either system. In the infrared condition, participants were seated in a fixed chair position in front of the Tobii Pro Spectrum and were instructed to maintain a relaxed upright posture and to keep their head as still as possible. In the webcam conditions, participants were instructed to face the webcam at eye level, to sit at about arm's length from the screen, and to keep their head as still as possible. Labvanced uses a virtual chin rest procedure that detects the participant's head position and prompts the participant to reposition their head when it deviates from the calibrated position.
table.lighting_conditions: Laboratory sessions (infrared and webcam) took place in the eye tracking laboratory of the chair under constant artificial lighting, with consistent conditions across participants. In the home condition, lighting could not be controlled. Participants were instructed to sit in a well-lit room and to make sure their face was evenly illuminated. Variability in lighting is one of the factors expected to contribute to differences between home and laboratory recordings (RQ2).
table.immediate_surroundings: Laboratory sessions took place in a quiet eye tracking laboratory with a standardized setup (fixed seating position, same screen, minimal distractions), and an experimenter was present to assist with calibration. In the home condition, participants completed the session without an experimenter present. They received written instructions to sit alone in a quiet space without distractions and to use the Google Chrome browser.
table.calibration_points: Both systems used a 9-point calibration, with calibration targets arranged in a 3 × 3 grid covering the screen (corners, edge midpoints, and center). In the infrared condition, the calibration was conducted in Tobii Pro Lab. In the webcam conditions, the built-in Labvanced calibration procedure was used, preceded by the Labvanced head position check. In the laboratory, the experimenter inspected the calibration results and repeated the calibration if it was insufficient; in the home condition, Labvanced prompted participants to repeat the calibration if it failed. No fixed numerical accuracy threshold was applied during data collection. Because accuracy and precision are themselves outcome variables of this study (H1a, H1b, H2a), recordings will not be excluded based on calibration accuracy for these analyses, as this would artificially reduce differences between the systems and between the recording environments. Recordings will only be excluded if the calibration could not be completed or if data loss exceeds the criterion specified in the data exclusion section.
table.area_of_interest_design: AOIs are defined on the classroom video vignettes and were created in prior work with the same video material (Pappa et al., 2020). Each student visible in the classroom (24 students in total) is covered by an individual AOI. As the primary AOI type, we use rectangular student-area AOIs that enclose each student's upper body, head, and desk area, since students are the central objects of attention in research on teachers' visual expertise. Additional AOIs cover the teacher and the learning materials (e.g., blackboard). Because the students and the teacher move during the videos, AOIs are dynamic, i.e., their position and size are adjusted over time to follow the respective person. All remaining screen areas are treated as non-AOI area. Identical AOI definitions are applied to the gaze data of both eye tracking systems. AOIs for the graph interpretation task are not part of the confirmatory analyses.
table.size_of_aois: Due to the perspective of the classroom camera, AOI sizes vary systematically with seating position: students in the front rows appear larger and are covered by larger AOIs than students in the back rows. The AOIs are comparatively large relative to the expected spatial error of both systems, which is the basis for our expectation in H1c that metrics based on these AOIs are robust to lower accuracy. The size of each AOI (mean, minimum, and maximum across the duration of each vignette) will be reported both in pixels and in degrees of visual angle for the laboratory setup.
table.distance_between_and_placement_of_aois: Students are seated in rows and are therefore placed close to each other, so that neighboring student AOIs are directly adjacent and partly separated only by small gaps; in the back rows, student AOIs can partly overlap due to the camera perspective. AOIs are drawn so that they do not overlap; where students occlude each other, the boundary is drawn along the visible outline of the student in front. The teacher AOI is located at the front of the classroom and the AOIs for learning materials are located at the blackboard. Because of the small distances between neighboring student AOIs, inaccurate gaze data can lead to AOI hits being assigned to a neighboring student. To quantify this, we will additionally report, as a sensitivity analysis, AOI hits on the level of seating rows and classroom areas (front, middle, back) in addition to individual student AOIs.
table.randomization: Randomization took place at the participant level and was conducted for two aspects of the design. First, participants were randomly assigned to one of the two recording environment groups: (a) both recordings (webcam-based and infrared) in the laboratory or (b) the webcam-based recording at home and the infrared recording in the laboratory. Second, the order of the two eye tracking systems (webcam-based first vs. infrared first) was randomized for each participant in both groups to control for order, learning, and adaptation effects. The order of the vignettes was identical in both sessions and for all participants. Assignment was made by the research team before the first session; participants had no influence on their group assignment or the order of the sessions.
table.explanation_of_foreknowledge_and_managin:
All data for this study were collected before this registration. Data collection was carried out by members of the project team, including a student research assistant. During data collection, the experimenters observed the system-specific calibration feedback in the laboratory sessions in order to decide whether a calibration had to be repeated, and the completeness of the recordings was checked to ensure that each session had been saved correctly. Beyond this, no data have been exported, preprocessed, visualized, or analyzed. In particular, no accuracy or precision values, no fixation- or AOI-based metrics, no descriptive statistics, and no comparisons between the eye tracking systems or the recording environments have been computed or inspected by any of the authors.

To limit unintended influences, the research questions, hypotheses, design, target sample size, and the core of the analysis plan described here are taken from the DFG project proposal and the ethics application, both of which were written before data collection started. Deviations from these documents in this preregistration (the formulation of H1c as an equivalence hypothesis, the separation of H2 into H2a to H2c, and the specification of preprocessing parameters and exclusion criteria) were made without access to the data. The data will not be accessed for analysis until this preregistration has been submitted. Any deviations from this plan will be reported transparently and justified in the resulting publications.
table.data_collection_procedures:
The target population consists of pre-service teachers, students of education-related study programs, and in-service teachers. Inclusion criteria were: being at least 18 years old and being enrolled in a teacher education program or an education-related program (e.g., educational science, educational psychology) or working as a teacher or educational professional. Persons without an educational or teaching-related background were excluded. As a precaution, pregnant persons were also excluded. Participation was possible in German or English; all materials were available in both languages.

Participants were recruited in the Munich area via university mailing lists (Technical University of Munich, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München), teacher education networks, contacts with schools, social media, and announcements in lectures and seminars. Interested persons received an e-mail invitation describing the study. Participation was voluntary, and written informed consent was obtained before the first session.

Each participant completed two eye tracking sessions, one with the webcam-based system and one with the infrared system, with at most two weeks between the sessions. Depending on their randomly assigned group, participants completed both sessions in the eye tracking laboratory at the Technical University of Munich or completed the webcam session at home and the infrared session in the laboratory. Participants in the home condition received written instructions on technical and environmental requirements in advance. After the eye tracking tasks, participants completed online questionnaires on demographics, experience with digital tools, and the usability of the recording procedure. Participants received 20 euros as compensation after completing both sessions. Data collection took place in 2025 and was completed before this registration.
table.sample_size: The unit of analysis is the individual participant, with repeated measurements nested within participants: each participant contributes one webcam-based and one infrared recording, each comprising five video vignettes. The target sample size was N = 84 participants; the final sample consists of N = 85 participants. Participants were randomly assigned to the two recording environment groups with a planned equal allocation (group 1: both recordings in the laboratory; group 2: webcam recording at home, infrared recording in the laboratory). Within each group, the order of the two eye tracking systems was randomized. The number of participants per group and the number of participants and vignettes remaining after the application of the exclusion criteria will be reported.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target sample size was determined by an a priori power analysis with G*Power 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007) for a repeated measures ANOVA with the within-subjects factor eye tracking system and the between-subjects factor recording environment, assuming a small-to-moderate effect size of f = 0.20, α = .05, and a power of 1 − β = .95. This analysis yielded a required sample size of 84 participants. The sample size was additionally constrained by the project budget (participant compensation for 84 participants). For the equivalence test of H1c, a sensitivity analysis shows that with N = 84 and equivalence bounds of d = ±0.30, the power to establish equivalence is approximately .73 if the true difference between the systems is zero. For the comparison of variances between the two recording environment groups (H2b), power is limited by the group sizes of about 42 participants each. We will therefore interpret non-significant results for these hypotheses with caution and report confidence intervals for all effect sizes.
table.stopping_rule: Before data collection started, the experimental procedure was piloted internally with four test runs (two webcam-based and two infrared sessions) to test the technical setup, the calibration procedures, and the instructions. Data collection began after the final adjustments based on this pilot. Pilot data are not included in the analyses. Data collection was terminated once the target sample size of 84 participants had been reached; sessions that had already been scheduled at that point were still conducted, resulting in a final sample of 85 participants. All 85 participants will be included in the analyses, subject to the preregistered exclusion criteria. The number of participants was not adjusted on the basis of any interim inspection of the data.
table.measured_variables:
Independent variables are the eye tracking system (webcam-based vs. infrared; within subjects) and the recording environment (laboratory vs. home; between subjects). The following variables are measured.

Data quality measures (primary outcomes for H1a, H1b, H2a):
(1) Accuracy: the mean angular distance (in degrees of visual angle) between the recorded gaze position and the position of known target points, computed from the gaze samples recorded while participants fixated the validation targets. Lower values indicate higher accuracy, i.e., a smaller systematic offset between recorded and actual gaze position.
(2) Precision: the root mean square of the angular distances between successive gaze samples (RMS sample-to-sample, in degrees of visual angle) during the fixation of the validation targets. Lower values indicate higher precision, i.e., less noise in the recorded gaze signal.
(3) Data loss: the proportion of samples without valid gaze data during the presentation of the video vignettes. Data loss is used to describe data quality and as an exclusion criterion.
(4) Effective sampling frequency: the mean number of recorded gaze samples per second. This is reported descriptively, since it is fixed for the infrared system and varies across participants for the webcam-based system.

Eye tracking metrics derived from the video vignettes (outcomes for H1c and H2b), each computed per participant and system and aggregated across the five vignettes:
(5) Number of fixations: the total number of fixations per vignette, indicating how often gaze pauses on parts of the scene.
(6) Mean fixation duration (in milliseconds): the average duration of fixations, commonly interpreted as an indicator of the depth of processing of the fixated information.
(7) Mean saccade length (in degrees of visual angle): the average distance between consecutive fixations, indicating how far the gaze jumps while scanning the classroom.
(8) Number of AOI hits: the number of fixations landing within the student, teacher, and learning material AOIs, indicating which parts of the classroom receive attention. AOI hits are computed per AOI and summed across student AOIs.

Questionnaire variables: demographics (age, gender, study program or profession, study phase or years of teaching experience), experience with digital tools, perceived usability of the recording procedure, perceived authenticity of the classroom videos, and, for the home condition, feedback on technical problems during the session. These variables are used descriptively and in exploratory analyses.

Graph interpretation task: gaze data recorded during the graph interpretation task are analyzed exploratively and are not part of the confirmatory hypotheses.
table.indices:
All derived variables are computed per participant and per eye tracking system.

Conversion to visual angle: Distances on the screen are converted from pixels into degrees of visual angle with θ = 2 · arctan(s / (2 · D)) · 180/π, where s is the distance on the screen in cm (pixel distance multiplied by the physical pixel size) and D is the viewing distance in cm.

Accuracy: For each validation target j, accuracy is computed as the mean angular distance between the n gaze samples recorded during the fixation of the target and the target position: A_j = (1/n) · Σ θ_i, where θ_i is the angular distance between gaze sample i and the target. The accuracy score of a participant is the mean of A_j across all validation targets.

Precision: For each validation target j, precision is computed as the root mean square of the angular distances between successive gaze samples: RMS_j = √[(1/(n − 1)) · Σ θ_(i,i+1)²], where θ_(i,i+1) is the angular distance between samples i and i+1. The precision score of a participant is the mean of RMS_j across all validation targets.

Data loss: For each vignette, data loss is the proportion of the vignette duration that is not covered by valid gaze data. It is computed as the summed duration of all gaps longer than 75 ms (intervals between consecutive valid samples, including the intervals before the first and after the last valid sample) divided by the vignette duration. The data loss score of a participant is the mean across vignettes.

Effective sampling frequency: f = (n_samples − 1) / (t_last − t_first), computed per vignette from the timestamps of the recorded samples (in seconds) and averaged across vignettes.

Eye tracking metrics: For each vignette, the number of fixations, the mean fixation duration, the mean saccade length, and the number of AOI hits are computed. The number of AOI hits is the number of fixations whose position falls within any of the defined AOIs (students, teacher, learning materials); AOI hits per individual AOI and per AOI category are reported descriptively. For each metric, the participant's score is the mean across all valid vignettes of the respective session.

Difference scores: For H2b and for the Bland-Altman analyses, a difference score is computed per participant and metric as Δ = metric(webcam-based) − metric(infrared). The standardized paired difference used for the equivalence tests in H1c is d_z = mean(Δ) / SD(Δ).

Questionnaire scales: Scale scores for usability, experience with digital tools, and perceived authenticity are computed as the mean of the respective items after reverse-coding negatively worded items. Scale scores are only computed for participants who answered at least 80% of the items of a scale.
table.eye_tracking_processing_algorithm: Raw gaze data (timestamps and x/y screen coordinates) of both systems are exported and processed with the same custom Python pipeline. Fixations are detected with a dispersion-threshold identification algorithm (I-DT; Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000), which is suitable for both high-frequency infrared data and low-frequency, irregularly sampled webcam data. A fixation is identified when consecutive gaze samples stay within a maximum dispersion of 1.0° of visual angle (dispersion computed as the sum of the horizontal and vertical range) for at least the minimal fixation duration. Fixation position is defined as the mean position of all samples belonging to the fixation. Adjacent fixations are not merged. Saccades are defined as the transitions between consecutive fixations, and saccade length is computed as the angular distance between the positions of consecutive fixations. Fixations are assigned to an AOI if the fixation position lies within the AOI in the video frame displayed at the onset of the fixation. Pixel distances are converted into degrees of visual angle based on the physical pixel size and the viewing distance (65 cm in the laboratory; for the home condition, an assumed viewing distance of 65 cm combined with the screen properties reported by the browser). The same algorithm and parameters are applied to the data of both systems and both recording environments. As a sensitivity analysis, all confirmatory analyses for H1c are repeated after downsampling the infrared data to the mean effective sampling frequency of the webcam-based recordings, in order to separate effects of spatial data quality from effects of sampling frequency. Accuracy and precision are computed from the raw, unprocessed gaze samples recorded during the validation procedures.
table.minimal_fixation_duration: The minimal fixation duration is 100 ms for both systems. At the typical sampling frequency of the webcam-based system of about 30 Hz, this corresponds to at least three consecutive gaze samples. Candidate fixations shorter than 100 ms are discarded and not counted as fixations.
table.upper_velocity_threshold: Not applicable for the confirmatory analyses, because fixations are detected with a dispersion-based algorithm (I-DT) rather than a velocity-based algorithm. Velocity-based algorithms are not used because they cannot be applied reliably to the low and irregular sampling frequency of the webcam-based system. For comparability with prior work using the same video vignettes, the infrared data will additionally be processed exploratively with a velocity-threshold algorithm (I-VT) with a velocity threshold of 30°/s.
table.gap_fill_in_functions_or_noise_reduction: Gaps in the gaze data of both systems with a duration of up to 75 ms (e.g., caused by brief signal loss) are filled by linear interpolation between the last valid sample before and the first valid sample after the gap. Longer gaps are not interpolated and are treated as missing data. No additional noise reduction or smoothing filter is applied to the data of either system, because noise is itself an outcome of this study (precision) and smoothing would affect the two systems differently. Any filtering that is applied internally by the recording software of the respective system cannot be switched off and is part of the system comparison. Accuracy and precision are computed from the raw data before gap filling.
table.statistical_tests:
All analyses are conducted in R. For each participant, all outcome variables are computed per system and aggregated (averaged or, for counts, summed and divided by the number of valid vignettes) across the five video vignettes. Alpha is set to .05. Within each hypothesis, the multiple outcome variables are treated as one family, and p-values are corrected with the Holm-Bonferroni procedure within each family. Directional hypotheses are tested one-sided.

H1a and H1b (accuracy and precision): For each of the two outcomes, a 2 × 2 mixed ANOVA is conducted with eye tracking system (webcam-based vs. infrared) as within-subjects factor and recording environment (laboratory vs. home) as between-subjects factor. H1a and H1b are supported if the main effect of system is significant and the infrared system shows lower values (i.e., better accuracy and precision) than the webcam-based system. Effect sizes are reported as partial η² and as Cohen's d_z for the paired difference, each with 95% confidence intervals.

H1c (eye tracking metrics): For each of the four metrics (number of fixations, mean fixation duration, mean saccade length, number of AOI hits), equivalence between the systems is tested with a paired two one-sided tests procedure (TOST) with equivalence bounds of d_z = ±0.30. Equivalence is concluded for a metric if both one-sided tests are significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction across the four metrics, i.e., if the 90% confidence interval of the standardized difference lies entirely within the bounds. H1c is fully supported if equivalence is established for all four metrics and partially supported if it is established for some of them. In addition, conventional paired t-tests are reported for each metric. As complementary measures of agreement between the systems, we report Bland-Altman analyses (mean difference and 95% limits of agreement) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC(2,1), absolute agreement) for each metric. The sensitivity analysis with downsampled infrared data repeats the TOST procedure.

H2a (data quality of the webcam system by environment): Accuracy and precision of the webcam-based recordings are compared between the home group and the laboratory group with one-sided Welch t-tests. H2a is supported if the home group shows significantly higher (i.e., worse) values than the laboratory group.

H2b (variability by environment): To separate variability caused by the recording environment from individual differences in gaze behavior, difference scores (webcam-based minus infrared) are computed for each of the four eye tracking metrics per participant. The variances of these difference scores are compared between the home group and the laboratory group with Brown-Forsythe tests (Levene's test based on the median). H2b is supported for a metric if the variance is significantly larger in the home group after Holm-Bonferroni correction across the four metrics. In addition, the variances of the raw webcam-based metrics are compared between the groups in the same way.

H2c (interaction): H2c is tested by the system × environment interaction in the mixed ANOVAs on accuracy and precision described for H1a and H1b. H2c is supported if the interaction is significant and the difference between the systems is larger in the home group than in the laboratory group. Significant interactions are followed up with simple effects tests of system within each group (Holm-Bonferroni corrected).

Assumption checks and robustness: Normality of residuals is checked with Q-Q plots and skewness and kurtosis values. Because accuracy and precision values are typically right-skewed, robust alternatives are used if skewness exceeds |2| or kurtosis exceeds 7: in this case, the mixed ANOVA is replaced by a robust mixed ANOVA on 20% trimmed means (bwtrim, WRS2 package), and the t-tests are replaced by Yuen's trimmed-means tests. Sphericity is not an issue because the within-subjects factor has only two levels. Homogeneity of variances between groups is not assumed for H2a (Welch tests). As a robustness check, all models for H1a, H1b, and H2c are repeated with session order (webcam first vs. infrared first) as an additional between-subjects factor; if order effects are significant, they will be reported and discussed.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participant level: Participants are excluded from all analyses if they did not meet the inclusion criteria, or if they withdrew their consent. Participants are excluded from the analyses of a given system if the recording of that session was not saved due to a technical failure, if the calibration could not be completed, or, in the home condition, if the session was completed on a tablet or smartphone. Participants with valid data from only one session are retained for analyses that only require data from that session (e.g., H2a for webcam data) and are excluded from all paired comparisons between the systems.

Vignette level: A vignette is excluded from a participant's session if data loss during that vignette exceeds 50%. For the paired comparisons of eye tracking metrics (H1c, H2b), only vignettes that are valid in both sessions of the participant are used, so that both systems are compared on the same stimulus material. Participants with fewer than three vignettes valid in both sessions are excluded from these analyses.

Data quality measures: Because accuracy and precision are outcome variables, no participant is excluded because of poor accuracy or precision values. Accuracy and precision are only treated as missing if valid gaze samples are available for fewer than five of the nine validation targets.

Outliers: No values are excluded as outliers, since extreme values in data quality are an expected and substantively relevant characteristic of webcam-based eye tracking. The influence of extreme values is handled by the robust procedures described in the statistical models (trimmed means if distributional criteria are violated). As a sensitivity analysis, all confirmatory analyses are repeated with a stricter vignette-level criterion (data loss above 25%).

The number of excluded participants and vignettes is reported separately for each system and recording environment, as the exclusion rates themselves provide information on the practical usability of webcam-based eye tracking.

For each metric, the participant's score is the mean across all valid vignettes of the respective session.

Difference scores: For H2b and for the Bland-Altman analyses, a difference score is computed per participant and metric as Δ = metric(webcam-based) − metric(infrared). The standardized paired difference used for the equivalence tests in H1c is d_z = mean(Δ) / SD(Δ).

A fixation is identified when consecutive gaze samples stay within a maximum dispersion of 1.0° of visual angle (dispersion computed as the sum of the horizontal and vertical range) for at least the minimal fixation duration. Fixation position is defined as the mean position of all samples belonging to the fixation. Adjacent fixations are not merged. Saccades are defined as the transitions between consecutive fixations, and saccade length is computed as the angular distance between the positions of consecutive fixations. Fixations are assigned to an AOI if the fixation position lies within the AOI in the video frame displayed at the onset of the fixation. Pixel distances are converted into degrees of visual angle based on the physical pixel size and the viewing distance (65 cm in the laboratory; for the home condition, an assumed viewing distance of 65 cm combined with the screen properties reported by the browser). The same algorithm and parameters are applied to the data of both systems and both recording environments. Accuracy and precision are computed from the raw, unprocessed gaze samples recorded during the validation procedures.", "The minimal fixation duration is 100 ms for both systems. No additional noise reduction or smoothing filter is applied to the data of either system, because noise is itself an outcome of this study (precision) and smoothing would affect the two systems differently. Any filtering that is applied internally by the recording software of the respective system cannot be switched off and is part of the system comparison. Accuracy and precision are computed from the raw data before gap filling.", "Both", "All analyses are conducted in R. Equivalence is concluded for a metric if both one-sided tests are significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction across the four metrics, i.e., if the 90% confidence interval of the standardized difference lies entirely within the bounds. ownership.dep_description: Eye tracking has become a key method in research on teachers' visual expertise, but studies have so far relied almost exclusively on infrared (IR) eye trackers in laboratory settings. text.text: Eye tracking is a key method in educational sciences, for example, in studying teachers' professional vision.
However, currently used infrared (IR) eye trackers confine research to small laboratory samples.
Webcam-based eye tracking could enable large online studies, but its data quality for educational contexts such as classroom video has to be empirically determined.
Seventy-nine participants viewed five classroom video vignettes twice, with a webcam-based system (Labvanced) and an IR system (Tobii Pro Spectrum).
Webcam recordings took place in the laboratory (n = 45) or at home (n = 34).
Webcam precision was markedly worse than IR precision (laboratory medians within fixations: 0.37° vs.
With identical processing, fixation counts, fixation durations, and saccade amplitudes were not equivalent across systems.

A more tolerant webcam threshold equalized fixation counts but not durations, and a noise-robust algorithm reversed the duration difference, so these measures reflect noise rather than viewing behavior.
After offset correction, dwell-time distributions on coarse grids agreed across systems (r = .73 for 4 × 4 cells).
It rested on regions all viewers attended to; individual deviations from this pattern were reliable within each system but did not correspond across systems.
At home, angular precision did not decrease, but the signal was noisier relative to the stimulus, and usability ratings were lower and more variable.

Webcam-based eye tracking can thus describe how attention is distributed across dynamic videos at a coarse scale, but neither individual differences in dwell time nor fixation-based measures are currently interchangeable with IR data.

Eye tracking is widely used in educational sciences, for example, to study teachers' professional vision, that is, how teachers notice and interpret classroom events (Seidel & Stürmer, 2014; Sherin, 2001).

text.text: Studies with classroom videos have shown, for example, that experienced teachers distribute their attention more evenly across students than novices (Seidel et al., 2021; Wolff et al., 2016).

text.text: A meta-analysis of 98 such studies, however, found that studies included on average only 13 in-service and 13 pre-service teachers (Keskin et al., 2024), too few to estimate individual differences reliably or to test moderators.

text.text: The bottleneck is largely technical: Infrared (IR) eye trackers are expensive, require trained staff and bind data collection to the laboratory.
Webcam-based eye tracking could remove this bottleneck.

Browser-based systems estimate gaze from a standard webcam on participants' own devices, which allows studies to be conducted remotely and at scale (Papoutsaki et al., 2016; Semmelmann & Weigelt, 2018).

text.text: Validation studies, however, have relied on fixation grids, natural images and visual-world paradigms with few, large regions of interest (Kaduk et al., 2024; Slim et al., 2024; Van der Cruyssen et al., 2024).

text.text: Video stimuli in educational contexts such as classroom videos are dynamic, visually dense and long, contain many socially relevant targets of varying size, and are analysed with measures such as fixation counts, dwell times on individual students or saccade amplitudes, which are sensitive to offsets and noise in the gaze signal.

To our knowledge, no study has compared webcam-based and IR eye tracking with these kind of stimuli and measures as used in applied educational science research, under both laboratory and home conditions, and with regard to how participants experience the recording.
Research with classroom videos relies on two families of measures (Grub et al., 2020; Keskin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Research with classroom videos relies on two families of measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Grub et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Keskin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Global measures, such as the number and mean duration of fixations and saccade amplitudes, depend on how fixations and saccades are segmented from the raw signal and thus on noise, sampling rate and data loss.
AOI-based measures, such as dwell time on individual students or the teacher, depend on whether gaze is assigned to the correct AOI and thus on systematic offsets relative to AOI size and spacing.

In classroom videos, AOIs are numerous, differ in size, sometimes overlap and move over time; at the same time, gaze in dynamic scenes tends to converge across viewers on socially salient regions (Smith & Mital, 2013).
text.formatted: In classroom videos, AOIs are numerous, differ in size, sometimes overlap and move over time; at the same time, gaze in dynamic scenes tends to converge across viewers on socially salient regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Smith & Mital, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Whether webcam-based eye tracking is robust enough is therefore not a single question but depends on the measure and on the spatial scale at which it is defined.

Data quality is usually described by accuracy, the systematic offset between true and recorded gaze position; precision, the variable error of the signal, commonly quantified as the root mean square of sample-to-sample distances (RMS-S2S); and data loss, together with temporal properties such as sampling rate (Dunn et al., 2024; Holmqvist et al., 2011 Holmqvist et al., , 2012)).

text.text: Offsets affect AOI-based measures depending on their size relative to AOI size and spacing, AOI assignment can be framed as a signal detection problem, and larger AOIs are more robust (Hessels et al., 2016; Orquin et al., 2016).

text.text: Noise affects event detection: Dispersion-based algorithms may split fixations into shorter ones or miss them, and velocity-based algorithms may detect spurious saccades (Blignaut, 2009; Hessels et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Noise affects event detection: Dispersion-based algorithms may split fixations into shorter ones or miss them, and velocity-based algorithms may detect spurious saccades <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blignaut, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hessels et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Webcam-based systems have no active illumination.

They locate the face and eyes in the image of a consumer camera and map appearance features to screen coordinates with a regression or deep-learning model calibrated for each participant (Kaduk et al., 2024; Papoutsaki et al., 2016).
text.formatted: They locate the face and eyes in the image of a consumer camera and map appearance features to screen coordinates with a regression or deep-learning model calibrated for each participant <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kaduk et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Papoutsaki et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Sampling rates are bounded by the camera frame rate, typically around 30 Hz, and accuracy depends on head pose, lighting and calibration stability.
Early work with the open-source library WebGazer found offsets of several degrees, delays of several hundred milliseconds and poorer data online than in the laboratory (Semmelmann & Weigelt, 2018).

text.text: Later studies replicated robust effects, but with smaller effect sizes and delayed time courses (Slim & Hartsuiker, 2023; Van der Cruyssen et al., 2024; Yang & Krajbich, 2021), and concluded that webcam studies are feasible when effects are large and regions of interest few and large.

text.text: Deep-learning-based systems have narrowed the gap: Labvanced reached a mean accuracy of 1.45° (EyeLink: 0.91°) with raw gaze correlations of about .80 to .90 (Kaduk et al., 2024), using an extended calibration with several head poses and a virtual chinrest that pauses the experiment when the head moves.

text.text: Three gaps remain.

Validations of current systems were conducted in the laboratory with short trials and simple stimuli; they reported signal correlations or replicated effects rather than the equivalence of derived measures; and they rarely compared laboratory and home recordings of the same participants.

Moving recordings from the laboratory to the home changes several factors at once that are constant in the laboratory but vary between participants at home: hardware such as camera position, screen size and processing power; physical conditions such as lighting and viewing distance (Hessels et al., 2015; Niehorster et al., 2018); behaviour such as head movements (Niehorster et al., 2018); and the absence of an experimenter who checks the setup or repeats a failed calibration.

text.text: These factors are expected to degrade data quality and, above all, to increase its variability between participants.
Evidence is mixed: Data quality was poorer online than in the laboratory in some studies (Bánki et al., 2022; Semmelmann & Weigelt, 2018) but not in others (Slim et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Evidence is mixed: Data quality was poorer online than in the laboratory in some studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bánki et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Semmelmann & Weigelt, 2018)</ref> but not in others <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Slim et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction between random and systematic error matters here.
If home recordings mainly add random error, group means remain unbiased and larger samples can compensate.

If they add systematic error that varies between participants, between-person differences in gaze become confounded with differences in setup, which would undermine the individual-differences questions that motivate large-sample research.
Testing this requires examining not only mean data quality but also the variance of system differences across participants.
Webcam-based studies also shift responsibility for the recording to participants, who must set up their device, complete a calibration and keep their head in position.
Technical problems are a main source of dropout and noise in online research (Sauter et al., 2020), and brief self-reports might help identify poor recordings.

text.text: For video-based educational research, perceived authenticity matters as well, because video tasks are valid only if viewers engage with the classroom situations as with real teaching (Blomberg et al., 2013; Codreanu et al., 2020).

text.text: We therefore assessed the perceived usability of the webcam recording and the perceived authenticity of the videos.
We compared a webcam-based system (Labvanced) with an IR reference system (Tobii Pro Spectrum) while participants viewed five classroom video vignettes.
Each participant was recorded with both systems; the webcam recording took place either in the laboratory or at home.
Research Question 1: Do data quality and derived eye-movement measures differ between webcam-based and IR eye tracking during classroom video viewing?
We expected better data quality for the IR system but derived measures that are largely robust to this difference, because classroom videos contain relatively large targets (Hessels et al., 2016).
text.formatted: We expected better data quality for the IR system but derived measures that are largely robust to this difference, because classroom videos contain relatively large targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hessels et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Hypothesis 1a (H1a): The IR system yields higher spatial precision than the webcam-based system.
Hypothesis 1b (H1b): Despite lower precision, the number of fixations, mean fixation duration and mean saccade amplitude are equivalent across systems, within equivalence bounds of dz = ±0.30.
Research Question 2: Does the recording environment (laboratory vs. home) affect the data quality of webcam-based eye tracking?
We expected poorer and, above all, more heterogeneous data quality at home.
Webcam recordings at home show lower precision than webcam recordings in the laboratory.
Webcam recordings at home show greater between-participant variability in the difference between webcam-based and IR measures than webcam recordings in the laboratory.
The difference in precision between the webcam-based and the IR system is larger for participants recorded at home than for participants recorded in the laboratory (System × Environment interaction).
Research Question 3: How do participants experience webcam-based recording in the laboratory and at home, and is this experience related to objective data quality?
We expected lower perceived usability at home.
We had no directional expectation for the perceived authenticity of the videos or for the relation between experience and data quality.

The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/s3afd), where processed data, analysis code and materials are available.

text.text: Data from eighty-four participants, predominantly master's students in education-related programmes, was collected.
The study used a mixed design with eye-tracking system (webcam-based vs.
IR) as a within-subjects factor and recording environment of the webcam session (laboratory vs. home) as a between-subjects factor.
All IR recordings took place in the laboratory.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two environments, and the order of the two systems was randomized within the laboratory group.

This yielded three groups: both sessions in the laboratory with the IR session first (n = 20) or with the webcam session first (n = 25), and the IR session in the laboratory followed by the webcam session at home (n = 34).
Webcam data were available for 81 participants.
For two participants, sessions were missing from the data export, and one participant did not complete the webcam session.

Two participants of the home group were excluded from all eye-tracking analyses, one because of an extreme IR validation error (114.7 mm; sample median 4.6 mm) and one because both recordings were largely incomplete.
Eye-tracking analyses were therefore based on 77 participants (45 laboratory, 32 home), and questionnaire analyses on 79 participants.
Participants who completed the questionnaire (n = 81) were on average 24.9 years old (SD = 3.3); 37 identified as female and 44 as male.
Participants viewed five video vignettes of authentic classroom instruction, presented in randomized order and at full screen.
The vignettes showed whole-class teaching situations with the teacher and a group of students visible, the typical stimulus format of professional vision research (Keskin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The vignettes showed whole-class teaching situations with the teacher and a group of students visible, the typical stimulus format of professional vision research <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Keskin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: They lasted on average 102 seconds, for a total viewing time of about 6 min, and were displayed at 1920 × 1080 px on the IR monitor.
Each trial ended with the end of the video.
Before the videos, participants were instructed: "You will watch five short videos showing typical classroom situations.
Please observe carefully what is happening in each scene.
There are no right or wrong observations.
Just try to take in what seems relevant and important to you."
The same five vignettes were shown in both sessions.
IR System.
IR data were recorded at 120 Hz with a Tobii Pro Spectrum integrated in a 23.8inch monitor (527 × 296 mm, 1920 × 1080 px), using Tobii Pro Lab.
Participants sat without a chin rest at a median eye-to-screen distance of 58 cm (IQR 52-63 cm).
A 9-point calibration was followed by a validation procedure.
Webcam-Based System.

Webcam data were recorded with the Labvanced platform, which estimates gaze in the browser on the participant's device with a deep-learning model and transmits only gaze coordinates (Kaduk et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Webcam data were recorded with the Labvanced platform, which estimates gaze in the browser on the participant's device with a deep-learning model and transmits only gaze coordinates <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kaduk et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Gaze was sampled at the webcam frame rate, nominally about 30 Hz (median inter-sample interval 32.0 ms in the laboratory and 33.4 ms at home), and reported in a fixed frame of 800 × 450 units, which the videos filled completely.

The session began with a calibration of 55 points in four head poses (about 2 min), which was repeated if the calibration error exceeded 10% of the screen diagonal; the session ended after three failed attempts.
During the videos, a virtual chinrest monitored head position, adaptive drift correction was active, and a short recalibration was presented every 120 s.
Devices whose face tracking ran below 7.5 Hz were excluded by the platform.
The study ran in full-screen mode in Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Opera on desktop or laptop computers; in the laboratory, Microsoft Edge on Windows was used.
Because frames were dropped (13% of intervals exceeded 50 ms), participants delivered a median of 26 valid samples per second in the laboratory and 30 at home outside recording interruptions.
In all sessions run in Edge, the last video of the sequence was recorded at about 15.6 Hz throughout (53 of 53 Edge sessions vs. 2 of 26 sessions in Chrome or Firefox).
In the laboratory, an external webcam (Logitech HD Pro C920 Full HD-Webcam 1920 x 1080) was attached to the same 23.8-inch monitor.
At home, participants used their own computers, with two exceptions laptops with an integrated camera.
Laboratory sessions were supervised by a trained experimenter who conducted the calibration.
Home sessions were unsupervised: Participants received a link and written instructions and completed the session at a time of their choosing.
In the laboratory, both sessions took place on the same day.
In the home group, the IR session always came first, and the webcam session followed after a median of 1.9 days (range 0-86 days).
Webcam sessions lasted a median of 20 to 23 min and IR recordings 14 to 17 min across groups.
After the webcam session, participants completed a questionnaire on their experience with the recording.
Questionnaire.

Usability of the webcam recording was assessed with five items on technical problems, the comprehensibility of the procedure, perceived tracking accuracy, difficulties with the webcam and perceived reliability of the tracking (α = .84).
A further item on feeling undisturbed was excluded because of a low corrected item-total correlation (r = .16).

Perceived authenticity of the classroom videos was assessed with six items on the realism of the videos, the ability to empathize with the situations, the clarity of the task, the ability to stay focused, the resemblance of one's perception to a real classroom situation and the appropriate length of the videos (α = .73).
Scale scores are item means.
Gaze data of both systems were transformed into stimulusrelative coordinates (0-1 relative to the width and height of the video area).
IR coordinates were referenced to the bounding box of the presented media and webcam coordinates to the 800 × 450 frame.
Stimulus-relative units require no assumption about screen size or viewing distance and are therefore comparable across environments.
Degrees of visual angle were computed for laboratory recordings, using the measured eye-to-screen distance for the IR system and a distance of 60 cm for the webcam.
Where angular values are reported for home recordings, a screen width of 30 cm and a viewing distance of 50 cm were assumed.
Fixation Detection.
Fixations were identified with the same dispersion-threshold algorithm (I-DT; Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000) for both systems, with IR data averaged to 30 Hz to match the webcam sampling rate.
text.formatted: Fixations were identified with the same dispersion-threshold algorithm (I-DT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Salvucci & Goldberg, 2000)</ref> for both systems, with IR data averaged to 30 Hz to match the webcam sampling rate.

text.text: The minimum fixation duration was 100 ms.

The dispersion threshold corresponded to 1.0° under the laboratory geometry and was applied as a fixed threshold in stimulusrelative units in both environments, so that it was identical relative to the stimulus.
On IR data, the implementation agreed with the manufacturer's I-VT classification (r = .91 for the number of fixations and r = .97 for mean fixation duration across 385 participant × vignette cells).

Data loss was the proportion of recording time during a vignette without a valid gaze estimate, with the expected number of samples based on 120 Hz for the IR system and on the median effective rate for the webcam.
For the webcam, recording time included interruptions in which the platform paused the video, for example during the timed drift corrections and when the head left the virtual chinrest.
Effective sampling rate was the reciprocal of the median inter-sample interval.
Precision was quantified in two ways.
Precision within fixations was the median root mean square of sample-to-sample distances (RMS-S2S) within detected fixations.
Because the spread of a fixation is bounded by the dispersion threshold, this conventional measure is constrained by the eventdetection parameters.
Threshold-free precision was the median RMS-S2S across sliding 200-ms windows; windows with fewer than four samples or with a gap longer than 2.5 times the median intersample interval were discarded.
Both measures were computed in stimulus-relative units and in degrees, with IR precision based on the 30-Hz samples.
Eye-Movement Measures.
For each vignette, we computed the number of fixations, the mean fixation duration and the mean saccade amplitude, defined as the distance between consecutive fixation centroids.

Spatial distributions were described by dwell-time proportions on regular grids over the video area (2 × 2 to 8 × 8 cells) and by attention maps, that is, duration-weighted fixation densities on a fixed 8 × 8 grid smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 0.75 cells).
A vignette was excluded if more than 50% of its samples were missing.

Paired comparisons between systems used only vignettes valid in both sessions, and participants with fewer than three such vignettes were excluded; analyses within one system applied the same criteria within that system.
No participant was excluded because of poor precision, and no outliers were removed, because extreme data quality values are a substantively relevant property of webcam-based eye tracking.
Analyses were conducted in R 4.5.1 (afex 1.5.0, effectsize 1.0.1, WRS2 1.1.7, psych 2.6.9, irr 0.85) and Python (pandas, scipy, statsmodels, I2MC 2.2.8).
Measures were averaged per participant and system across valid vignettes; count measures are expressed per vignette.
Within each hypothesis, outcomes formed one family and were corrected with the Holm-Bonferroni procedure.
Directional hypotheses were tested one-sided.
Each precision measure was analysed in stimulus-relative units with a 2 × 2 mixed ANOVA with system as within-subjects factor and environment as between-subjects factor.
H1a corresponds to the main effect of system, H2c to the System × Environment interaction.
We report partial η² and Cohen's dz with 95% confidence intervals.
If skewness exceeded |2| or kurtosis exceeded 7, a robust mixed ANOVA on 20% trimmed means was decisive (Wilcox, 2017).

text.text: H1b.

Equivalence of the number of fixations, mean fixation duration and mean saccade amplitude between systems was tested with paired two one-sided tests (TOST; Lakens, 2017) with equivalence bounds of dz = ±0.30.

text.text: Webcam precision was compared between environments with one-sided Welch t tests in stimulus-relative units and, for threshold-free precision, additionally in degrees under the assumed screen geometries.
H2b was tested on within-person difference scores (webcam minus IR) for each eye-movement measure, whose variances were compared between environments with Brown-Forsythe tests.

To examine the dependence of fixation measures on the dispersion threshold, the webcam threshold was varied from 1.0° to 3.0° in steps of 0.25° with the IR threshold fixed at 1.0° (ratios of means with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, 5,000 resamples of participants).
As an event-detection algorithm designed for noisy data, I2MC (Hessels et al., 2017) was applied to both systems on a common 30-Hz grid with a minimum fixation duration of 100 ms.
text.formatted: As an event-detection algorithm designed for noisy data, I2MC <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Hessels et al., 2017)</ref> was applied to both systems on a common 30-Hz grid with a minimum fixation duration of 100 ms.

text.text: For grid AOIs, webcam gaze was corrected for a participant-specific positional offset, estimated as the median difference between webcam and IR gaze positions in the other four vignettes.
Because all viewers of a video tend to look at similar regions, agreement can arise without individual information.

We therefore also compared each participant's webcam data with the IR data of other participants viewing the same video (200 random assignments), correlated participant-specific deviations of dwell-time proportions from the video mean across systems, and estimated the split-half reliability of these deviations within each system (alternating 5-s segments, Spearman-Brown corrected).
Attention maps were compared with Pearson correlations and by the percentile rank of each participant's own IR map among the IR maps of all participants (.50 = chance).
Robustness.

Hypothesis tests were repeated with session order as an additional factor within the laboratory group, with a stricter vignette-level criterion of 25% data loss, with IR data at the native sampling rate and with a webcam dispersion threshold corresponding to 1.5°.
Usability and authenticity ratings were compared between environments with Welch t tests, with Hedges' g and 95% confidence intervals as effect sizes, and their variances with Brown-Forsythe tests.

Relations between usability and webcam data quality during video viewing (data loss and both precision measures) were estimated within each environment and as partial correlations controlling for environment; because of ceiling effects, rank correlations are reported in addition.
Under the 50% criterion, 34 of 225 webcam vignettes in the laboratory (15.1%), 27 of 160 webcam vignettes at home (16.9%) and 21 of 410 IR vignettes (5.1%) were excluded.
Eight participants (three laboratory, five home) had fewer than three valid paired vignettes, which left 69 participants for the system comparisons (42 laboratory, 27 home).
Analyses within one system included 45 laboratory and 27 home participants for the webcam and 42 and 32 participants for the IR system.
Under the 25% criterion, 57 participants remained for the system comparisons (36 laboratory, 21 home).

With a webcam threshold of 1.5°, no measure became equivalent; the webcam then detected more fixations and shorter saccades than the IR system, and the difference scores for precision within fixations were more variable at home (variance ratio 2.48, Holm-corrected p = .048).
Grid AOIs.

After correction for a participant-specific positional offset estimated from the other four vignettes, agreement of dwell-time proportions between systems was r = .69 for a 2 × 2 grid, .74 for 3 × 3 and .73 for 4 × 4, and declined to .62, .59, .54 and .49 for 5 × 5 to 8 × 8 grids (Figure 4; n = 42 participants, 175 vignettes).

Agreement was only slightly lower when the webcam data of each participant were compared with the IR data of other participants viewing the same video (r = .67, .70 and .71 for 2 × 2 to 4 × 4 and .44 for 8 × 8).

Participant-specific deviations from the video mean were reliable within each system (IR: .70 to .80; webcam: .81 to .89 for 2 × 2 to 8 × 8 grids) but corresponded only weakly across systems (r = .06 to .20; 3 × 3: r = .20 [.07, .30]; 4 × 4: r = .08 [-.03, .20]), also after correction for unreliability (.08 to .23).
An offset estimated from the same vignette raised this correspondence only to r = .27.

Attention Maps.

Attention maps of the same participant recorded with both systems correlated at a median of .49 (laboratory .48, home .50), hardly more than maps of different participants recorded with the two systems (.47).
A participant's own IR map was not more similar to their webcam map than the IR maps of other participants (mean percentile rank .53, p = .066 against chance).
Maps of different participants correlated at .93 within the IR system and at .21 (laboratory) and .37 (home) within the webcam system.
Usability ratings were high overall but lower and more variable at home than in the laboratory (Table 4); the variance at home was 3.8 times larger, F(1, 77) = 13.97, p < .001.

Lower usability went along with more webcam data loss in both environments (partial r controlling for environment = -.30, p = .008) and, at home, with noisier gaze signals (threshold-free precision: r = -.40, p = .039; laboratory: r = .10, p = .53), but rank correlations were weaker (data loss: ρ = -.19, p = .106; precision at home: ρ = -.11, p = .58).
Precision within fixations was unrelated to usability (partial r = -.10, p = .43).

Webcam-based eye tracking captured how attention was distributed across classroom videos at a coarse spatial scale, but neither individual differences in where participants looked nor how their gaze unfolded in fixations and saccades.
Webcam precision was 2.6 times worse than IR precision within fixations and, comparing medians, five times worse without a fixation threshold.
With identical processing, fixation counts, fixation durations and saccade amplitudes were not equivalent across systems and did not agree at the level of individuals.

Dwell-time distributions on coarse grids, by contrast, agreed substantially once participant-specific offsets were corrected, but individual deviations from the common viewing pattern did not correspond across systems.
At home, angular precision did not decrease, but the signal was noisier relative to the stimulus, and participants rated the procedure as less usable.
The precision gap matches the difference in measurement principle (Holmqvist et al., 2012; Kaduk et al., 2024); more informative is how it propagated to derived measures.

text.text: A more lenient dispersion threshold equalized fixation counts but not durations, which remained below the IR values even at 3.0°: Noise breaks long fixations into short segments separated by spurious displacements, as predicted for dispersion-based algorithms on noisy data (Blignaut, 2009; Hessels et al., 2017).

text.text: That most webcam fixations lay at the minimum duration of the algorithm, that webcam saccade amplitudes were tightly coupled to fixation counts and that a noise-robust algorithm reversed the direction of the duration difference shows that webcam fixation measures are determined by the algorithm and the signal rather than by viewing behavior.
They cannot be compared with IR measures, not even in direction, and should currently not be interpreted as indicators of processing depth or expertise (Keskin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: They cannot be compared with IR measures, not even in direction, and should currently not be interpreted as indicators of processing depth or expertise <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Keskin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Spatial measures were more robust.

Dwell-time distributions on grids up to 4 × 4 cells correlated at about .73 across systems, with lower agreement for finer grids, in line with the noise robustness of large AOIs (Hessels et al., 2016; Orquin et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Dwell-time distributions on grids up to 4 × 4 cells correlated at about .73 across systems, with lower agreement for finer grids, in line with the noise robustness of large AOIs <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hessels et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Orquin et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This required a participantspecific offset correction; without it, agreement did not exceed r = .45.
Two results qualify the agreement.

First, it rested on regions that all viewers attended to: Gaze converges across viewers in dynamic scenes (Smith & Mital, 2013), and the webcam data of one participant agreed almost as well with the IR data of others.

text.text: Second, individual deviations from this common pattern were stable within both systems but did not correspond across systems.
The webcam thus recorded a consistent, participant-specific pattern that differed from the IR pattern.

Because an offset estimated from the same video improved correspondence only slightly, this points to participant-specific distortions beyond a constant shift, such as offsets that change between videos or compressed or stretched gaze distributions, which can arise from calibration, head pose and camera position (Kaduk et al., 2024).

text.text: Webcam dwell times therefore describe how attention is distributed across a scene, but differences between viewers in webcam data cannot be equated with differences in viewing, which is what expertise comparisons rely on (Keskin et al., 2024).

text.text: Home recording did not reduce angular precision, in line with Slim et al. (2024) and in contrast to earlier findings (Semmelmann & Weigelt, 2018); the calibration and head-pose handling of the Labvanced system may absorb part of the environmental variation.

(2024)</ref> and in contrast to earlier findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Semmelmann & Weigelt, 2018)</ref>; the calibration and head-pose handling of the Labvanced system may absorb part of the environmental variation.

text.text: Relative to the stimulus, however, home recordings were noisier, by a factor that the smaller visual angle of the videos on laptop screens fully explains, so studies with small screens should choose AOI sizes accordingly.
System differences were not more heterogeneous at home.
The 13-ms difference in mean fixation duration corresponds to a third of a sample per fixation and does not indicate a difference in viewing behavior.
Environment was, moreover, confounded with camera type and browser.

Most participants experienced the webcam recording as unproblematic, but the home setting split them: Usability ratings were lower and about four times as variable, and only home participants rated the procedure as clearly problematic, in line with the concern that online settings add variation between participants more than they shift the average (Sauter et al., 2020).

text.text: Perceived authenticity did not depend on the environment, which supports online settings for video-based research in educational science.
Usability ratings tracked data loss and, at home, signal noise only weakly; a brief usability check can flag problematic recordings but cannot replace objective indicators of data quality.
The results suggest six recommendations for researchers who want to move educational studies on professional vision, or other studies with video stimuli, online.
First, prefer spatial over temporal measures.

Dwell-time proportions on sufficiently large AOIs describe how attention is distributed across a scene; measures based on fixation segmentation, especially fixation duration, should not be compared across systems or pooled with IR data.
Differences between viewers should only be interpreted once it is shown that they reflect differences in viewing.
Second, match the method to the stimulus.
Large, dynamic classroom scenes can be studied with webcams, also at home.
Whether this extends to pages with small, adjacent or peripheral regions, such as graph or text-based tasks, needs to be tested separately.
Third, use large AOIs and test their size.
Agreement depended strongly on AOI size.
AOI size should be reported in stimulus units and results tested across AOI definitions, taking into account that small screens increase noise relative to the stimulus.
Fourth, include validation targets.
Short validation sequences before and after each stimulus allow accuracy to be estimated and participant-specific offsets and distortions to be corrected from independent data.
Fifth, treat event detection as part of the method.
Identical parameters do not guarantee comparable measures across systems with different noise levels, and different algorithms can even reverse system differences.
Precision within fixations is bounded by the dispersion threshold and should be complemented by a threshold-free measure.
Several limitations qualify these conclusions.

First, environment was confounded with camera type and browser, and the home group always completed the IR session first; analyses restricted to laboratory participants with the same order led to the same conclusions.

Second, screen size and viewing distance were not controlled at home, so stimulus-relative noise cannot be separated from screen geometry, and angular values for home recordings rest on assumed geometries..
Third, the effective sampling rate depended on browser and device; vignettes recorded at half the rate were largely excluded, and analyses without them led to the same conclusions.

Webcam-based eye tracking in educational sciences can describe the spatial allocation of attention in classroom videos at a coarse scale, and it can do so at home without loss of angular precision or perceived authenticity.
Differences between viewers, however, are confounded with stable, participant-specific measurement errors, and fixation-based measures are not interchangeable with those of IR systems.

For professional vision research, webcam-based eye tracking is therefore best seen as a scalable complement for questions about how attention is distributed across dynamic classroom scenes, not as a replacement for laboratory eye tracking when individual differences or the timing and structure of gaze matter.
